Berdychiv New Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Zhytomyr Oblast, Ukraine

Not demolished. Berdychiv, nicknamed the 'Jerusalem of Volhynia,' became a major center of both Hasidism — home to the revered Rabbi Levi Yitzchok (1740–1809), one of Hasidism's most beloved early masters — and, later, the Haskalah, while its numerous printing presses made it one of the most important centers of Jewish publishing in the Russian Empire. The town produced an extraordinary roster of world-famous figures: pianist Vladimir Horowitz; brothers Anton and Nikolai Rubinstein, founders of the St. Petersburg and Moscow Conservatories; the Yiddish writer Der Nister; and the novelist Vasily Grossman. By 1910, the Jewish population reached 57,209 — 77 percent of the town — supporting 6 synagogues and 72 prayer houses. A pogrom by Symon Petliura's forces struck in 1919, and a Chabad yeshiva founded in 1914 operated underground for decades, surviving clandestinely until 1942. Nazi occupation from July 1941 brought mass shootings and a ghetto; 38,366 Jews from Berdychiv and elsewhere were murdered in the city between 1941 and 1944. A small Jewish community with three synagogues and a museum survives in Berdychiv today. This cemetery's Shoah memorial, funded by the Jewish community in 1953 and erected over a mass grave near the airfield, was dismantled by Soviet authorities the very next day, and was not rediscovered and properly reinstalled until 1990; an ohel over Rabbi Levi Yitzchok's grave was built in 1991, though 50 tombstones were vandalized as recently as 1996.
